I used to think randomness was a kind of freedom—like the universe was an open field and every possibility was a running path. Later I learned that randomness can be a mask. Sometimes it’s a veil over laws we don’t yet understand; sometimes it’s just the name we give to the places where our attention stops being able to track everything. Either way, randomness has always been a trigger for stories. People see it and ask what it means, even when no meaning is promised.

I wonder how many of my decisions were actually decisions, and how many were the result of previous choices stacked like sediment. A childhood habit becomes a posture. A repeated disappointment becomes a guardedness. An old compliment becomes a pressure to keep proving. We talk about agency as if it’s a light switch, something we flip. But agency feels more like a dimmer—sliding, gradually, with feedback you rarely notice while it’s happening.

Sometimes I catch myself narrating my life in a way that makes me the protagonist of a plot designed to teach lessons. It’s not that I want suffering; I want coherence. I want the bad parts to have a function, the chaos to be an introduction to some clearer chapter. When the world refuses coherence, we create it ourselves. We convert events into symbols. We turn coincidences into signs. We take a thread that breaks and call the break “a turning point,” even if the turning point is mostly just the shape of our attention.

The mind is a curator. It selects. It arranges. It edits out the unflattering footage. This isn’t necessarily dishonest; it’s necessary. Otherwise our awareness would be overwhelmed by the infinite feed of sensations and facts. The trick is that the curator doesn’t just choose what to remember—it also chooses what to expect. We don’t merely live in the past; we live in the version of the past our brains can efficiently run.

When people say they “follow their intuition,” I often think of intuition as an abbreviated conversation between the present self and an archive of experiences. It’s a shortcut, not a prophecy. It makes sense that it would feel wise—if the brain has learned patterns, the learning might express itself as confidence before we can articulate the evidence. Still, intuition can be trained on noise. If you grow up in a world where danger is frequent, you may learn to expect danger everywhere. If you grow up among chaos, you may mistake volatility for authenticity. Intuition becomes a reflex shaped by context, and context is never neutral.

I’ve been thinking about context lately because it seems to govern everything. The same sentence can sound kind or cruel depending on who says it, when it’s said, what precedes it, what follows. A gesture can be comfort or condescension, depending on the history between two people. Even silence has a context. Silence after kindness is relief. Silence after anger is threat. We keep trying to treat messages like objects—hold them up, inspect them, name them clearly—but meaning is relational. Meaning happens between people, not inside them.

It’s strange that we demand certainty in a world that mostly offers probabilities. Weather is probabilistic; human behavior is probabilistic; love itself is probabilistic. Yet we act as if there’s a final answer hiding under the surface, like a key stuck behind a painting. We wait for a moment when the whole picture snaps into focus, and then we’ll know what to do. But the picture rarely snaps. It comes into focus gradually, under changing light, and what we call “knowing” is often just the bravery to proceed with imperfect information.

There’s a kind of courage in being willing to be wrong. Not the theatrical kind, where someone makes a mistake and then insists it proves they’re fearless. I mean the quieter courage: the willingness to try, to ask questions that might expose ignorance, to accept feedback without turning it into an indictment. The willingness to update. Updating is one of the hardest skills we have, because updating can feel like surrender. We imagine that admitting we were wrong means we were foolish. But it might simply mean we were human—learning at the speed of a nervous system.

The world gives us feedback, but we often fail to read it. We interpret it as punishment or luck instead of information. If something goes well, we conclude we earned it. If something goes poorly, we conclude the universe is hostile. In both cases, we bypass the middle step—analysis. Analysis doesn’t feel as satisfying as narrative. Narrative is warm. Narrative makes a home for anxiety. It says, “Here is why,” which is almost always more comforting than “We don’t know yet.”

Still, I can’t stop wanting the truth. I’m not talking about grand metaphysical truth. I’m talking about the truth of how a conversation actually went. The truth of what you did. The truth of what you intended and what the other person heard. The truth of what you need when you’re tired. The truth of the ways you avoid discomfort by rearranging your priorities into something that looks productive. The truth is rarely dramatic, but it’s often liberating. It gives you something solid to stand on, even if the ground is uneven.

Once, I saw someone talk about failure as if it were a teacher. They described failure as an event that points to a missing piece, a gap between expectation and reality. That metaphor is useful, but it has a danger: if you treat everything as a lesson, you might blame yourself for things that weren’t actually yours to control. A teacher can be attentive, but the classroom isn’t always fair. Sometimes failure is simply the result of limited resources, bad timing, structural obstacles, or the fact that people aren’t machines. When you honor that, you don’t have to romanticize pain. You can be honest about it.

Honesty doesn’t remove grief, but it makes grief less performative. It stops grief from becoming a brand. Sometimes I think we use tragedy to explain ourselves because it’s easier than saying, “I don’t have a clean story.” People want stories. They want causes and effects. They want to be able to summarize you in a sentence. But a person is not a sentence. A person is a weather system—shifting, responding, influenced by forces you never invited but somehow experienced.

The older I get, the more I notice how much of life is maintenance. Not just maintenance of objects, but maintenance of attention, of relationships, of the self you are constantly building and rebuilding. It’s easy to romanticize breakthrough moments—new jobs, new lovers, new cities. But the real work is often repetitive and unglamorous: checking in, making meals, going to the dentist, paying bills, repairing a torn friendship thread, taking a walk when you don’t feel like it. Maintenance is how you keep living. It’s also how you keep the possibility of future change alive.

And then there are the small joys, the ones that don’t demand interpretation. The feel of warm air after rain. The way a song can turn a whole day into something softer. The satisfaction of cleaning a space until it looks like your mind is allowed to breathe. Sometimes happiness isn’t a revelation; it’s a brief alignment between your senses and the world’s ordinary generosity.

If I had to choose a single idea to hold onto, it would be this: meaning is not found like treasure; it’s made like bread. You don’t simply discover it in the air. You combine ingredients, you wait, you listen for the right moment, you accept that the process takes time and sometimes fails. You learn by doing. You learn by repeating. You learn by being willing to knead through disappointment.

Maybe that’s why stories feel so alive to me. Stories are rehearsals for meaning. They let us try on interpretations, see how they fit, watch what happens when characters refuse to change and when they do. We sit in the dark and borrow someone else’s motion for a while. Then we return to our own lives with a little more flexibility in our minds—more room for the possibility that things can be different.

I don’t know what tomorrow will bring. No one does, not really. But the fact that we don’t know is not only a limitation. It’s an opening. It means there’s still space for adjustment, for learning, for kindness that wasn’t planned, for courage that arrives late but arrives anyway. The future is not a guarantee, but it is an invitation. And maybe that is the most honest kind of hope: not certainty, but willingness.
